tip: 비가 와요 (biga wayo) = 'rain comes' – how Korean says it's raining.
Everyday Korean says 'have' with 있어요 (isseoyo = exists): 우산 있어요? (usan isseoyo?) literally asks 'does an umbrella exist?'
눈이 와요 (nuni wayo) = it's snowing. On its own 눈 (nun) is both snow and eye - context decides.
아무것도 (amugeotdo) needs a negative verb with it: 아무것도 안 해요 (amugeotdo an haeyo) = I do nothing at all.
푹 (puk) = deeply, and it usually goes with resting: 푹 쉴 거예요 (puk swil kkeoyeyo) = I'm going to rest up.
편 (pyeon) counts movies and shows: 두 편 (du pyeon = two films).
Monday-morning Korean: 잘 쉬었어요? (jal swieosseoyo? = did you rest well?)
배터리가 없어요 (baeteoriga eopseoyo) = 'no battery' = my phone's dying.
놓고 왔어요 (noko wasseoyo) = left it behind – the forgot-it phrase.
Korean often builds a verb by adding 하다 (hada) to a noun: 카톡해요 (katokaeyo) = to message on KakaoTalk.
You don't 'take' photos in Korean – you 찍다 (jjikda), the snap-a-shot verb: 사진을 많이 찍었어요 (sajineul mani jjigeosseoyo) = took lots of photos.
셀카 (selka) = 'self-camera' = selfie – a Konglish classic.
이불 (ibul) = blanket or bedding, and you tidy it rather than make it: 이불을 정리해요 (ibureul jeongnihaeyo).
끓이다 (kkeurida) = boil something up: 라면을 끓였어요 (ramyeoneul kkeuryeosseoyo) = I made ramyeon.
제일 (jeil) = most or best: 제일 좋아요 (jeil joayo) = it's the best.
아파요 (apayo) = it hurts, and the sore part takes 이/가: 머리가 아파요 (meoriga apayo) = my head hurts.
열이 나요 (yeori nayo) = literally a fever comes out, which is how Korean says you have a fever.
기침을 많이 해요 (gichimeul mani haeyo) = literally do a lot of coughing; many symptoms pair with 하다 (hada).
감기에 걸렸어요 (gamgie geollyeosseoyo): catching a cold takes 에 (e), not 을 (eul).
몸살 (momsal) = the whole-body ache of a bad cold, and it breaks out rather than gets caught: 몸살이 났어요 (momsari nasseoyo).
속 (sok) = your insides: 속이 안 좋아요 (sogi an joayo) = I feel queasy.
안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) = it isn't working: 소화가 안 돼요 (sohwaga an dwaeyo) = my digestion isn't working.
못 (mot) before a verb = cannot: 못 일어나요 (mon nireonayo) = I can't get up.
-아서 / -어서 (-aseo / -eoseo) = because: 아파서 (apaseo) = because it hurts.
-ㄹ 것 같아요 (-l geot gatayo) = I think it will happen: 토할 것 같아요 (tohal geot gatayo) = I feel like throwing up.
-고 (-go) also links two states with no time order – 어지럽고 열도 나요 (eojireopgo yeoldo nayo) is just 'dizzy and feverish', not one thing then another.
때문에 (ttaemune) after a noun = because of: 기침 때문에 (gichim ttaemune) = because of the cough.
Someone senior with a title usually takes 께 (kke), not 한테 (hante): 부장님께 (bujangnimkke) = to the department head.
-ㄹ게요 (-lkkeyo) = a promise to the listener: 쉴게요 (swilkkeyo) = I'll rest, promise.
For someone you respect, the verb usually adds -시- (-si-): 걸리셨어요 (geollisyeosseoyo) rather than plain 걸렸어요 (geollyeosseoyo).
